title: Editing Video by Chatting With AI

sections.heading: An Everyday Analogy
sections.body:
Think of old video editing like cutting paper film with scissors on a timeline.

Prompt-based video editing is like telling an assistant what you want. You type "remove silences, make it brighter, add captions" and the AI does the cuts for you.

Transcript-based editing means the video turns into text. Delete a word in the text, and that part of the video disappears.

sections.heading: Why It Exists
sections.body:
Traditional tools like DaVinci Resolve, iMovie, and CapCut need manual timeline work. That takes time and skill.

These new tools exist to make editing faster with simple chat commands. They use:
- AI avatar cloning: a digital copy of you that can speak any script
- Text-to-video generation: creating video from just written text
- Automated cuts and silence removal: AI finds and removes pauses and bad takes

This helps creators make avatar videos, translations, and voiceovers quickly.

sections.heading: What Can Go Wrong
sections.body:
AI editing is fast, but it has limits.

An avatar clone can look fake or steal someone's face and voice without permission. Auto-cuts can remove important pauses or emotion. Chat commands may misunderstand you and cut the wrong part.

Term to know: prompt means the written instruction you give the AI, like "cut the boring parts." If the prompt is vague, the result will be wrong.

steps.narration: You write a simple instruction like remove silences.
The AI turns your words into editing tasks.
It cuts, adds captions, or uses your avatar clone.
You watch and fix any mistakes the AI made.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x and everyone uses AI avatar cloning?
options: Viewers trust drops and fake clones spread
quiz.why: At huge scale, fake copies and trust issues break first, plus auto-cuts and voiceovers can make errors.
